title: ASME Audit Support: NDE Level III for Code Stamp Shops
description: Prepare the NDE side of your ASME joint review: written practice, Section V procedures, subcontractor control and records. Talk to a Level III today.
h1: ASME Certification Audit Support: Level III Help with the NDE Portion of Your Joint Review
html:
This page is for quality managers and QC managers at ASME Code shops preparing for a new or renewal Certificate of Authorization review, and for the NDE subcontractors who examine their welds. Atlantis NDT works as your outside ASNT NDT Level III. We review and fix the NDE parts of your quality control system, from the manual section and the written practice to Section V procedures, personnel records, subcontractor controls and calibration, and then rehearse the demonstration with your people before the ASME team and your Authorized Inspector arrive. Ask for ASME audit support; we reply within one business day.

What the ASME certification review actually is

ASME does not certify individual vessels. It accredits the quality control system of the manufacturer or assembler that builds them. A shop holding a Certificate of Authorization may apply the ASME Certification Mark with the designator for its scope, and that mark tells the buyer and the jurisdiction that the item was built under an accepted system and inspected by an Authorized Inspector. Applications are made through ASME's CA Connect portal. The shop also needs an inspection agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency (AIA), and CA Connect has a step for confirming that agreement.

The on-site part is called a joint review. An ASME team leader runs it, your AIA takes part, and a jurisdictional or National Board representative may join; that is also how a shop holding both an ASME certificate and a National Board R certificate can have the two reviewed together. Of the five phases ASME lists (a desk read of your manual before the visit, an opening session with a plant walk, implementation, a private team session, and the exit meeting), implementation is the one that decides the outcome. You must show the whole system working on an item for each designator you want, including real welding when welding is in scope. If there is not enough live Code work in the shop, a mock-up is used. ASME runs certification on a three-year period, and for a renewal the team leader asks for a list of all Code work done since the previous review.

Deficiencies found during implementation can be corrected on the spot. Anything still open at the exit meeting leads to a re-review or a follow-up visit, and a deficiency touching past or current Code work needs documented disposition. A gap in NDE personnel records or subcontractor control usually reaches back into work already shipped, which is why it deserves attention months ahead.

Designators and the NDE each one brings

The NDE load in a review depends on what you build. This table is a planning aid, not a substitute for the Code Section itself.

DesignatorCode Section and scopeNDE that usually appears in the demonstration
USection VIII Division 1 pressure vesselsRadiography of butt welds to the extent the design joint efficiency requires, or ultrasonic examination where the Division permits it in place of radiography; MT or PT where the material, thickness or detail calls for it
U2Section VIII Division 2 (alternative rules)Examination set by the Division 2 examination groups, typically more volumetric NDE than Division 1, with UT of welds common
U3Section VIII Division 3 high pressure vesselsHeavy-wall forgings and welds, with ultrasonic examination of material and welds at the centre of the plan
S, A, E, MSection I power boilers, boiler assembly, electric and miniature boilersVolumetric examination of boiler butt welds under Section I rules; assembly certificate holders show NDE of the welds they make in the field or shop
PPSection I pressure piping, including boiler external piping to ASME B31.1RT or UT of piping butt welds and surface examination of branch and attachment welds as the rules require
H, HLWSection IV heating boilers and lined potable water heatersA lighter NDE load; the review leans on welding, visual examination and the pressure test, but any NDE the manual claims must still sit under a procedure
PRTParts fabrication under Sections I, IV, VIII and XIIWhatever examination the part requires before it ships to the certificate holder who completes the item

ASME also issues RP for fiber-reinforced plastic vessels, T for Section XII transport tanks, and Section XIII designators for pressure relief devices (V, HV, UV, UD, UV3, UD3, TV and TD), where the review centres on testing rather than weld NDE.

Where NDE sits in your quality control system

ASME's general guide for review teams breaks the quality control system into fifteen items. Nondestructive examination is item 9, calibration of measurement and test equipment is item 11, and records retention is item 12. Item 1 asks for control features that demonstrate Code compliance, including subcontracted activities, which is where NDE subcontractors are caught. Item 14 covers the Authorized Inspector.

For NDE, the guide expects the shop to have a way of identifying the NDE procedures that apply to its Code scope and of making sure NDE personnel are qualified to the requirement of the applicable Code Section. NDE procedures must be demonstrated or qualified to the Authorized Inspector, and the Inspector has the right to ask for proof that NDE personnel can perform and interpret the examinations specified. Interpretation reports and radiographic film must be retained, and NDE equipment must be calibrated.

Reviewers read the manual first and then follow it onto the shop floor. A manual that says the right things while the floor does something different is the most common way an NDE section fails. If your manual also carries ISO 9001 language, ASME's joint review description asks that non-ASME provisions be clearly identified, because they lengthen the review and can generate findings of their own. Our NDT audit consulting page explains how we test a manual against the floor before the team does.

NDE personnel: what the Code asks and what the reviewer samples

The Code Section you build to decides the personnel rules, and Section V Article 1 supplies the framework those rules point back to. In Section VIII Division 1, personnel who perform and evaluate radiography, and ultrasonic examination of welds, must be qualified and certified to their employer's written practice, with ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189 used as the guideline for that practice. For magnetic particle and liquid penetrant work under the Division's mandatory appendices, the manufacturer certifies that each examiner passes an annual near-vision and color-contrast check and is competent in the technique, the interpretation and the evaluation. Many shops put MT and PT under the same written practice as RT and UT. Check your certified edition, because this wording has moved over time.

A reviewer typically picks names off a recent NDE report and asks for the trail behind each:

  • the written practice in force on the date of the examination, with the SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition it is based on and the Level III who approved it;
  • the certification statement for that person, method and level, signed by the employer;
  • training hours and experience hours that meet the written practice, with evidence rather than a single total;
  • general, specific and practical examination records with grades, dates and the examiner's name;
  • a near-vision record that was current on the examination date, and a color-contrast record;
  • for the Level III, the credential and the scope of methods covered.

Atlantis drafts or revises written practices, rebuilds training records and certificates, documents experience logs and sets up vision examination records. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own people, so a course certificate alone never satisfies a reviewer; our SNT-TC-1A based Level II training supplies the training hours, and the employer completes the certification. To check hours by method, use the SNT-TC-1A hours planner.

NDE procedures and the demonstration to the Authorized Inspector

Section V requires a written procedure when the referencing Code Section calls for one, demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Inspector. That demonstration is not a reading exercise. A qualified technician performs the examination to the procedure on a representative weld, shows the calibration or sensitivity check, covers the required volume or surface, and records the result the way the procedure says.

Each method article adds its own content. Article 4 lists essential and nonessential variables for ultrasonic procedures, and when the referencing Code Section requires procedure qualification, a change to an essential variable means requalifying. Article 2 governs radiographic technique: source or tube, film or digital system, image quality indicator selection and placement, density or contrast limits, and identification. Acceptance standards come from the construction code, not Section V, so a procedure citing Section V alone is incomplete. Article 1 ties the two together.

What an Inspector watches for during a demonstration: the procedure revision on the floor matches the one approved in the manual system; the calibration block is the material and thickness the procedure names and carries its certificate; the technician can explain scanning coverage and reference level; MT and PT steps such as surface preparation, dwell time, field direction and light intensity are actually measured rather than assumed. We write and correct NDE procedures and technique sheets and run procedure demonstrations as dry runs. Common reasons procedures get rejected are collected in this article on Section V procedure rejections.

Subcontracted NDE: the part of the manual most shops get wrong

Most small and mid-size stamp shops subcontract radiography, and many subcontract UT as well. That is acceptable to ASME, but the responsibility does not move with the work. ASME's joint review description is explicit: when NDE is subcontracted, the records qualifying the subcontractor's procedures and people have to be on hand where the review takes place. If those files sit in the subcontractor's office, the review stalls.

A workable subcontractor section in the manual answers these questions:

  1. How is an NDE company evaluated before it goes on the approved supplier list, and how often is it re-evaluated?
  2. Who in the shop reviews and accepts the subcontractor's written practice, procedures and personnel certifications, and where is that acceptance recorded?
  3. What does the purchase order flow down: Code Section and edition, method, extent of examination, acceptance standard, procedure approval and record content?
  4. Who reviews radiographs and reports for acceptance on behalf of the certificate holder before they go to the Authorized Inspector?
  5. How do film, digital images and reports come back to the shop, and who keeps them?
  6. How are subcontractor technicians working inside your shop checked on arrival?

Atlantis audits NDE subcontractors against those controls through our subcontractor approval audits. Radiography in the United States requires a license under 10 CFR Part 34 or the matching Agreement State regulation, which Atlantis does not hold, so Atlantis does not shoot film there and your RT stays with a licensed radiography company. As a Level III we can review that company's radiographs and RT procedures for you, and our report validation service checks reports against the procedure and acceptance criteria.

Records, film and calibration

The records item in the review covers the Manufacturer's Data Reports, radiographs and other records the Code Section requires. For NDE that means each report should identify the item and weld, the procedure and revision, the technician and level, the equipment serial number and its calibration status, the acceptance standard applied, the result, and the reviewer who accepted it. The manual should say how long film, digital images and reports are kept, who holds them when a subcontractor made them, and how the Inspector reaches them.

Calibration control has to cover every piece of examination, measuring and test equipment used to meet a Code requirement. For NDE that includes ultrasonic instruments and their linearity checks, transducers, calibration and reference blocks with material certifications, densitometers and density step wedges, light meters for black light and white light, MT yokes and their lift-test weights, and thermometers used to confirm PT temperature limits. A densitometer without a current calibration record makes every density reading on every film open to question. If calibration lives in a spreadsheet, the equipment calibration guide shows how to stop out-of-date items reaching the floor, and the certificates app keeps personnel certifications and vision dates in one place.

Getting the demonstration item right

For a U certificate the demonstration item is often a small vessel or mock-up with longitudinal and circumferential seams and a nozzle. Its NDE should come from the drawing, not be added for show. A clean demonstration looks like this:

  • the traveler or inspection plan shows where NDE is required and where the Inspector holds the job;
  • the NDE is ordered on a purchase order or work order that names the procedure, the extent and the acceptance standard;
  • qualified personnel examine the weld to the approved procedure, with calibrated equipment;
  • the shop's reviewer accepts or rejects the result and records it before the Inspector reviews it;
  • any rejectable indication goes through repair, re-examination and nonconformity control, which is itself good evidence of item 7, correction of nonconformities;
  • the reports, film and personnel records can all be produced at the review table.

The weak link is usually the hand-off between the subcontractor's report and your own acceptance, so that is where our walk-through starts.

NDE findings review teams write most often

  • The manual names a written practice or procedure revision that is not the one in use.
  • Personnel certified to a written practice that cites an older SNT-TC-1A edition than the manual claims.
  • Near-vision records lapsed for one or more technicians who signed recent reports.
  • Experience hours entered as one figure with no supporting evidence.
  • Subcontractor procedures and certifications never reviewed or accepted by the certificate holder.
  • No evidence that procedures were demonstrated to the Authorized Inspector.
  • UT procedures missing essential variables required by Article 4, or a variable changed without requalification.
  • Radiographs accepted with an image quality indicator that is not visible or not the required designation.
  • Calibration blocks with no material certificate, or instruments past their calibration date.

Piping work under the stamp program

Boiler external piping built to ASME B31.1 falls under Section I administrative rules, so it is fabricated by a holder of the appropriate certificate, usually the PP designator, with Authorized Inspection. ASME's joint review description lists B31.1 among the scopes demonstrated for PP. Your NDE controls for that piping are the same as for boiler work. See our B31.1 summary.

ASME B31.3 process piping has no ASME certificate or designator. A vessel shop may still fabricate B31.3 spools under its own quality system, and the owner's inspector, not an ASME Authorized Inspector, oversees examination. That code places examiner qualification records with the employer and sets its own acceptance criteria. Keep the two code paths visibly separate in your procedures so a reviewer never finds a B31.3 acceptance table on a Section VIII job. The B31.3 summary covers its examination rules.

What Atlantis does, and where the line sits

What we do for an ASME review is all NDE: gap review of the NDE, calibration and records sections of the manual; written practice and procedure work; personnel record clean-up; subcontractor audits; a mock review of the NDE items; and help writing corrective action evidence after the real review. Anoop Rayavarapu founded Atlantis; his ASNT NDT Level III certification covers five methods (UT, RT, MT, PT and VT), and he has 11+ years of field experience across several countries.

Where the line sits:

  • Atlantis is not ASME, not an Authorized Inspection Agency and not your Authorized Inspector. The review team and ASME decide.
  • Atlantis does not hold an ASME Certificate of Authorization and does not stamp anything. Your shop owns its quality control system.
  • Welding procedures, procedure qualification records and welder qualifications stay with your shop's welding engineer; Atlantis does not author or qualify any of them. For how those fit together, read WPS, PQR and WPQ explained and our Section IX summary.
  • Nuclear construction under Section III and its N-type certificates is outside our scope; Atlantis does not provide NQA-1 or other nuclear quality-assurance services.
  • Atlantis does not calculate remaining life or perform fitness-for-service assessments.

How an engagement runs

  1. Document request. You send the items listed below; the first pass is mostly remote.
  2. Desk review. A Level III reads the manual's NDE, calibration, records and subcontractor sections against your Code Section and ASME's review guide, then samples personnel and procedure records.
  3. Gap report. Each gap is written as a finding with the evidence a reviewer would ask for, ranked by whether it touches shipped Code work.
  4. Fixes. We draft revised manual text for your approval, rewrite procedures, rebuild records and audit subcontractors as needed.
  5. Mock review on site. Atlantis sends a Level III to your shop to walk the demonstration item, interview technicians and sample records as the team will.
  6. After the review. If the team leaves NDE deficiencies, we help assemble corrective action evidence for the AIA follow-up or re-review.

Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad and supports shops elsewhere by travel and online. Regional pages cover shop clusters and state jurisdiction notes in Houston, Tulsa, Baton Rouge, Birmingham, Charlotte, Chicago, Milwaukee, Cleveland, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. Repair organizations should also read our NBIC R-stamp audit support page.

What to send us

  • Your current quality control manual, or at least the NDE, calibration, records, subcontractor and Authorized Inspector sections, with its revision status.
  • Your certificate scope and designators, the review date if set, and any findings from the last review or AIA audits.
  • The NDE written practice and the list of certified personnel by method and level.
  • NDE procedures and technique sheets, with evidence of demonstration to the Inspector where you have it.
  • Your approved NDE subcontractor list and the qualification files you hold for each.
  • Calibration register for NDE equipment and blocks.
  • A sample job package with NDE reports, so we can test the trail end to end.

For a broader document review, see NDT audit documentation, Level III documentation services and outsourced Level III consulting.

faq.q: Does ASME require our NDE technicians to be certified to SNT-TC-1A?
faq.a: It depends on the Code Section and method. Section VIII Division 1 requires radiography and ultrasonic personnel to be certified to the employer's written practice, using SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 as the guideline, while MT and PT examiners under its appendices need a manufacturer's certification of vision and competence. Most shops cover every method under one written practice to keep it simple.

faq.q: Can we subcontract all of our RT and UT and still pass the joint review?
faq.a: Yes, provided your manual controls the subcontractor and you can produce its procedure and personnel qualification files at the review. The certificate holder stays responsible for the work. Our subcontractor approval audits build the file the team will ask for.

Your written practice names who approves them, normally a Level III in the method. The procedure must also be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Authorized Inspector where Section V or the construction code requires it. Atlantis can write the procedure and act as the reviewing Level III; your shop releases it under its own system.

faq.q: What does a procedure demonstration to the Authorized Inspector involve?
faq.a: A qualified technician performs the examination to the written procedure on a representative weld while the Inspector watches calibration, coverage, technique and recording. Keep a signed record of each demonstration. We rehearse these through our procedure demonstration service.

faq.q: Can Atlantis act as our outside Level III?
faq.a: Yes. Many stamp shops have Level II technicians but no Level III on staff. Atlantis can serve as the outside Level III named in your written practice for UT, RT, MT, PT and VT: approving procedures, preparing and grading examinations, and reviewing records. Your company still certifies its own personnel.

faq.q: Will Atlantis attend the joint review with us?
faq.a: We can be on site if you want a Level III available to explain the NDE program, but the review is between your shop, the ASME team and your AIA. Most clients get more value from the mock review a few weeks earlier, when there is still time to fix what we find.

faq.q: Do you write the welding procedures for our demonstration item?
faq.a: No. Welding procedure specifications, procedure qualification records and welder qualifications belong to your shop and its welding engineer under Section IX. Atlantis works on the NDE side of the program. See WPS, PQR and WPQ explained.

faq.q: Can you help with a nuclear N-type certificate?
faq.a: No. Section III nuclear certificates and the nuclear quality-assurance programs behind them are outside Atlantis's scope, and we do not offer NQA-1 support.

faq.q: Can Atlantis radiograph the welds on our demonstration vessel?
faq.a: Not in the United States, because Atlantis holds no radioactive-materials or x-ray license for field radiography there. Your licensed radiography company shoots the film, and Atlantis can review the radiographs and the RT procedure as a Level III. UT, MT, PT and VT are methods Atlantis can carry out at customer sites.

faq.q: How far ahead of the review should we start?
faq.a: Start as soon as the review is likely, ideally several months out. Written practice changes, new examinations and vision checks take calendar time, and a subcontractor that needs to send records needs notice. Send your manual and we reply within one business day with the next steps.

faq.q: We already have NDE deficiencies from the review. Can you still help?
faq.a: Yes. We review the deficiency wording, identify the root cause in your NDE program, and help you assemble corrective action evidence for the AIA follow-up or a re-review. Where the deficiency affects past Code work, we help you document how that work was evaluated.
